dialog.body: Public Works, this is Lorraine. Good afternoon, how can I help you?
Hi, yes, so it did it again after the storm, and now I'm looking at it out my window and it's just sitting there. The whole street. You know what I'm talking about, right?
Okay, I'm going to back up a little, because I don't have the first part. What's sitting there, and where are you calling from?

Oh, sorry. The water. The street in front of my house turned into a pond after the nor'easter, last weekend, Saturday into Sunday. It's Wednesday and it's still there. I'm at 426 Broadway, in the North End.
426 Broadway, North End. And the water's still standing in the road, three days after the storm ended?
Standing, yes, and the cars come through and they're throwing wakes, like boats. Real waves. [line breaks up] up onto the sidewalk. I'm worried they're going to push it into the house.
You broke up on me for a second. You said the cars are throwing wakes up onto the sidewalk, and you're worried about the water reaching the house. Did I get that right?
Yes, that's right. I'm on speakerphone, I'm sorry, my hands are full of papers. Can you hear me okay now?
I can hear you fine now. Is there water up against the house at the moment, or is it just the street?

Just the street so far. It's about to the top of the curb, though. And there's something else. There's a manhole cover right out front and it looks off. Like it's sitting up an inch, or it's crooked, I don't know. It wasn't like that before.
A manhole cover that looks raised or shifted by about an inch. Is it in the travel lane, where cars are driving over it?
Yes, right in the lane. Cars hit it and I hear a clunk. I haven't gone out to touch it, I'm not going near that water.
Good, please don't. I'll make a note that it's in the lane and that you hear it clunk when cars go over. That's a safety item, so I'll flag it.
Okay. Can I ask, is that a city drain or a state one? Because somebody told me Broadway might be the state's.

Fair question. Some of the bigger roads do belong to the state. I don't know offhand which this stretch is, so I'll have the crew check what it is. If it turns out to be the state's, we'll pass it along to them. You don't have to chase that part.
Okay, good, because I wouldn't know who to call. I'd be on the phone all day.
That's our job. Now, do you know if the drain in front of your house is clogged with leaves or debris? Can you see a grate under the water?
I can't see anything, it's all brown water. There was a lot of leaves and sand at the corner before the storm. And somebody said I should fill out the farms, to report it?
The farms? Oh, forms. Sorry, I thought you meant something else for a second. You don't need to fill out any forms. I'm taking the report right now over the phone, and that's all it takes.
Oh, good. Forms, yes, that's what I said. I thought there'd be paperwork.

No paperwork on your end. Let me read back what I have. 426 Broadway, North End. Standing water in the street since the nor'easter, Saturday into Sunday, still there today. Cars are throwing wakes onto the sidewalk. A manhole cover in the travel lane looks raised about an inch. Is that all correct?
That's all correct. Yes.
Okay. And is anyone else on your block having it, or is it just the low spot out front?
I think the neighbors are the same. The house next door has a puddle all the way across their driveway. I haven't asked everyone.
That helps. I'll note the neighbor's driveway too. Can I get a number in case the crew needs to reach you?
401-555-0160. And the name?
Conceicao Cabral. C-O-N-C-E-I-C-A-O. Cabral, C-A-B-R-A-L.
Conceicao Cabral. Got it. Is there anything about the manhole cover that makes it look dangerous, like a gap you can see down into, or is it just sitting high?
Just high on one side, I think. I can't tell for sure because of the water. That's why I'm nervous. If a car hits it wrong, or a kid, or somebody walking.

I understand. I'm marking it as a priority because of the traffic over it. If anything changes, say the cover moves more or there's a gap, call back right away. And if it ever looks like a real hazard, you can call the police non-emergency line so they can put something out there.
Okay. And how long, do you think, before somebody comes? The water's been there three days.

The crews have been working through a long list since the storm, so I'd say within the next day or two for someone to look at it. If they can clear the drain, the water should go down fairly quickly after that.
Okay. A day or two. I'll watch it, and if it gets up on the lawn I'll call again.
Please do. Is there anything else you wanted to report while I have you?
No, that's it. Thank you for being patient with me. I jumped right in without even saying hello.
No trouble at all. Thanks for calling, Ms. Cabral. Stay out of that water, and we'll get someone out there.
Thank you. Bye now.
